title: Lift up your gates (Psalm 23 [24])
hook: the earth is the Lord's, and the king of glory comes in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord ruleth me, the shepherd psalm in the Douay. Your line was I shall want nothing. What turned out to be enough? Today, a psalm with a procession in it. Day one hundred sixty-four.

Picture a crowd climbing a hill toward a walled city, singing. At the front, carried on poles, is the ark, the gold-covered chest that Israel believed was the throne of the invisible God. They reach the city gates, and the gates are shut. So the crowd outside calls up to them. And the watchmen on the walls call back a question. And the crowd answers. It's call and response, like a stadium chant, and Psalm 23 in the Douay, 24 in most Bibles, may well be the script for that moment.
screen: `A CROWD CLIMBING A HILL.` → `THE ARK AT THE FRONT.` → `THE GATES ARE SHUT.`

segments.voice: It opens wide: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." Everything. The ground, the sea, every person on it. Saint Paul quotes this line to settle an argument about food: eat what's sold in the market, he says, because the earth is the Lord's. Then the question at the foot of the hill: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord: or who shall stand in his holy place?" And the answer isn't a bloodline or a title. "The innocent in hands, and clean of heart." Clean hands, meaning what you do. A clean heart, meaning what you want. Then the gates. "Lift up your gates, O ye princes, and be ye lifted up, O eternal gates: and the King of Glory shall enter in." And from the wall, the challenge: "Who is this King of Glory?" And the crowd: the Lord who is strong and mighty. It happens twice, like a chant that builds. Christians have heard Christ in this psalm for a very long time. Some heard his entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday. Some heard the Ascension, the gates of heaven opening. And an old Christian story tells of Christ going down to the dead on Holy Saturday, and the gates of the underworld hearing this very psalm before they break. For centuries, on Palm Sunday, the procession would stop outside the shut church door, someone would knock with the foot of the cross, and the gates would be sung open.
screen: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `CLEAN HANDS, CLEAN HEART.` · `WHO IS THIS KING OF GLORY?` · `THE DOOR KNOCKED WITH A CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a window or a door on purpose. If you can reach one, go and open it now, slowly, and stand there. If you can't, picture a door in your home and imagine opening it wide. Settle, and breathe the outside air. Think of the psalm's first line: the earth is the Lord's, the street, the neighbors, the weather, all of it. If you pray, you can say, lift up your gates, and let God in. If you don't, let the open door be a way of welcoming the day. The bell holds the time.
Lift up your gates. The psalm's cry at the city wall, so the King of Glory can come in. Today's word.
Your line: the earth is the lord's. Today, walk one ordinary street and remember that every bit of it belongs to someone other than you. Day one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 23 [24] in the Liturgy of the Hours, sometimes as the opening Invitatory psalm, and hear it at Mass in Advent and on feasts like the Presentation of the Lord.

original.note: Latin: lift up your gates, the psalm's cry in the Vulgate, sung in chant and processions for centuries.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old line about city gates.
what it means: a call and response at the wall, so the King of Glory can come in.
what a scholar hears: probably a liturgy for bringing the ark into Jerusalem, and later read by Christians of Palm Sunday, the Ascension and Christ breaking the gates of death.

sources.ref: Gospel of Nicodemus (Descent into Hell), ch. 5

notes: Douay Psalm 23 wording: confirm against a Challoner edition.
The ark procession setting is a common scholarly reconstruction (cf. 2 Samuel 6), hedged 'may well be'.
Harrowing of hell: the Gospel of Nicodemus (Descent into Hell) uses Psalm 24's gate dialogue; described as 'an old Christian story', not scripture. Confirm.
Palm Sunday rite before 1955: the subdeacon knocked on the closed church door with the processional cross while the Gloria, laus was sung (the dialogue drew on Attollite portas). Confirm details.
